title: I vibe-coded a mobile game until the codebase got too complicated for vibe coding to work. So I vibe-coded a tool that tells me when that's about to happen again.
author: ch3ch3ch3n
selftext:
A while back I posted here about vibe-coding a mobile game for my wife (Godot + Claude Code + ElevenLabs, zero ads, zero IAP, just a dog you dress up in increasingly absurd designer accessories). That part went fine. The game shipped, it's playable free in-browser, she likes it.

What I didn't post about is what happened next, because it wasn't fun to write about at the time.

As the game grew past a toy project, the same workflow that built it started quietly breaking it. Not in ways a linter would catch. The agent would rename something in one file and miss a caller two files away. It would edit a string that a router somewhere else was matching against, and the mismatch wouldn't show up until I ran the game and a screen just didn't load. A member I'd moved during a refactor was still being read by code that hadn't been told it moved. Nothing crashed at write time. Nothing crashed at compile time, if there even was a compile step. It just quietly stopped working the way I expected, and I'd spend twenty minutes tracing a bug that a linter had cheerfully passed.

The pattern, once I saw it, was obvious: a linter reads a file. The stuff that was breaking lived in the seams between files, string contracts, scene connections, the boundaries my own [AGENTS.md](http://AGENTS.md) claimed existed but nothing was checking. Every fix was a patch on a symptom, not the actual gap, which is that agents are very good at editing the file in front of them and have no idea what else in the codebase is quietly depending on it staying the same shape.

So instead of vibe-coding another CRUD app or wrapper or second game, I vibe-coded a tool that answers one question before I let an agent touch anything: **what happens when the next agent edits this?**

It's called VibeCheck. It's an auditor for codebases built with AI agents, no dependencies beyond Python 3.9 and git, nothing leaves your machine unless you explicitly opt into a model-assisted review. It doesn't call an LLM by default. It traces string contracts across files (a screen name passed to a router, an event name looked up in a handler table, a key read out of a save file), checks the boundaries your own docs claim exist against the actual dependency graph, flags members that no longer exist after a rename, catches build traps (like a compile-time preload of a file your export filter strips, which looks fine on your desk and is a blank screen on the device), and picks up stale prompt debris agents leave behind in your docs.

**How a vibe coder actually uses it:**

Three commands do basically everything:

    python3 -m vibecheck scan .

Point it at your repo. You get a self-contained HTML report: a Vibe Debt Score across six categories, a "Do Not Let AI Touch This" ranking of your riskiest files, a dependency graph, and a blast-radius box you can type any planned change into.

    python3 -m vibecheck blast . "replace the inventory system"

This is the one I actually use every day. Before I hand an agent a task, I run this with a plain-English description of the change. It spits out a brief: which files the change will probably touch, what's likely to break and why, what to read first, and the invariants to preserve (with the actual lines that pin them). I paste that straight into Claude Code or Codex as context before it starts editing. It turns "the agent confidently broke something three files away" into "the agent had the seam mapped out in advance."

    python3 -m vibecheck check . --fail-on high

A CI gate. Exit 1 if there's an agent-risk finding at or above the severity you set, with file:line so you know exactly what to look at.

I didn't want to just claim this works, so I backtested it against the real commit history of the game that broke in the first place: 41 commits, 21 eligible ones, each scanned only using history that existed at that point in time, then scored against what that commit actually touched. Predicting the file a commit changed most, VibeCheck hit 0.48 recall@5 and 0.65 recall@10, ahead of static-graph-only, co-change-only, and same-directory guessing, and well ahead of random. It's a one-repo sample size, so take it as "better than a coin flip and better than guessing by folder," not gospel.

It's GDScript/Godot-native since that's where it was born, with full support for Python too and a language-agnostic tokenizer for everything else (JS/TS, C#, Go, Rust, Swift, shaders).

Links:

* VibeCheck: [https://github.com/chehlee-stack/vibecheck](https://github.com/chehlee-stack/vibecheck)
* The game that broke first: [https://ch3ch3ch3n.itch.io/brownies-world-tour](https://ch3ch3ch3n.itch.io/brownies-world-tour)

If you've hit the same wall, agent output looking fine file by file while the codebase quietly rots at the seams, I'd genuinely like to hear how you're catching it, because "just read the diff more carefully" stopped scaling for me a while ago.
